title: Check a job offer before acting
summary: Pause and independently verify the employer, recruiter, role, and contact details before sharing information or money.
warning_signs: An unexpected recruiter contacts you through an encrypted messaging app.
The role promises high income for little effort or has almost no hiring process.
You are asked for money, cryptocurrency, bank access, or identity documents early in the process.
example: A person receives an unexpected work-from-home offer, is moved to a messaging app, and is asked to pay before earnings can be released.
best_practices: Find the employer's official website independently and contact it using details you find yourself.
Do not pay money or send banking, cryptocurrency, or identity details to an unverified recruiter.
Take time to check the offer with someone you trust.

title: Do not pay to start a job
summary: Up-front recruitment, training, equipment, task, or account top-up payments are important job-scam warning signs.
warning_signs: A fee is required before work or training begins.
You must top up an account or cryptocurrency wallet to unlock tasks or earnings.
The recruiter promises the payment will be reimbursed later.
example: A supposed supervisor asks a candidate to pay for a training kit and promises reimbursement in the first pay cheque.
best_practices: Do not send an up-front payment to obtain work or release earnings.
Contact your bank quickly if you have already transferred money.
Report the account and offer to the platform and Scamwatch.

title: Verify recruiters and protect identity details
summary: Unexpected contact, messaging-only interviews, and early requests for sensitive identity information deserve independent checking.
warning_signs: The recruiter insists on WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, or personal email only.
There is no formal interview or discussion of qualifications and references.
Passport, driver licence, banking, or other identity details are requested before verification.
example: A recruiter uses the name of a real company but communicates only through a personal account and requests passport and bank details.
best_practices: Contact the company using an independently sourced official phone number or website.
Do not rely on links or contact details supplied in the message.
Limit personal details in a resume until the recruiter is verified.

title: Check information before trusting or sharing it
summary: Question the source, evidence, context, headline, and motive, then compare the claim with trustworthy independent sources.
warning_signs: The headline does not match the content or uses strong emotion without evidence.
The author, date, original context, or supporting sources are missing.
The content presents a one-sided claim as settled fact.
example: An old image is reposted with a new caption that claims it shows a current event in a different place.
best_practices: Check the original source, author, publication date, and full context.
Compare the claim with multiple trustworthy sources before sharing.
Use reverse image search or a recognised fact-checking service where appropriate.
source_name: eSafety Commissioner - Fake news and misinformation

title: Respond safely to suspicious messages
summary: Phishing messages imitate trusted people or organisations to obtain information, money, credentials, or device access.
warning_signs: A message pressures you to click, open an attachment, scan a code, or act urgently.
The sender requests passwords, verification codes, banking details, or personal information.
The displayed sender or link looks familiar but is not the official address.
example: A message that appears to come from a bank links to a copied login page and asks for account credentials.
best_practices: Do not use links or contact details in the suspicious message.
Open the official app or type the official address yourself to verify the request.
Report the message and secure affected accounts quickly if information was shared.

title: Recognise common pressure and impersonation patterns
summary: Scams often combine authority, urgency, emotion, scarcity, or an unusually attractive offer to reduce the time you spend checking.
warning_signs: The sender claims authority and demands immediate action.
The offer seems unusually rewarding, scarce, or too good to be true.
You are discouraged from checking with another person or official source.
example: A caller impersonates a trusted organisation, creates urgency, and directs payment through an unusual method.
best_practices: Stop and give yourself time before sending money or information.
Check the request through an official channel you find independently.
Protect accounts and report the incident promptly if something went wrong.
source_name: Australian Cyber Security Centre - Recognise and report scams
